newsitem.title: USA: Senate votes to allow seeing-eye dogs in chamber.
newsitem.headline: Senate votes to allow seeing-eye dogs in chamber.

text.p: The Senate, acting swiftly to defuse an emotional controversy, agreed on Tuesday to allow disabled people to bring guide dogs, wheelchairs and other equipment they need into the chamber.
The decision followed a dispute that arose Monday when a visually impaired aide to Oregon Democratic Sen. Ron Wyden was prevented from bringing her guide dog onto the Senate floor.
The Senate is selective about who is allowed into the chamber and has no formal rules governing dogs. That meant consent of all senators was needed to allow the animal onto the floor.
An unnamed senator objected to Wyden's request, barring his aide, Moira Shea, from entering with her guide dog Beau.

Wyden protested that the move was contrary to protections provided by the Americans with Disabilities Act. Two years ago, lawmakers voted for the first time to make Congress comply with federal health, safety and other workplace laws.

Tuesday, Republican Leader Trent Lott asked the Senate to give its sergeant-at-arms authority to allow guide dogs and other support services into the chamber on a case-by-case basis, while a committee considered an official change of the rules.
Lawmakers agreed to Lott's request with no fuss.
"I commend the majority leader for his expeditious handling of the matter," Senate Democratic Leader Tom Daschle said.
He said the decision represented a "sensitivity to the issue and a recognition of the need for some practical application of our current rules."
